questions.q: What does .agg() let you do that plain .count() from Lesson 53 doesn't?
options: Compute multiple different statistics per group — like sum, average, and max — all in one call
Nothing extra; they are exactly identical in every case
.agg() can only be used without groupBy() at all
.agg() replaces groupBy() entirely and cannot be combined with it
questions.explain: count() only ever counts rows; .agg() takes as many aggregate functions as you want in a single call.

questions.q: What happens when you call .agg() on a DataFrame with no groupBy() beforehand?
options: It treats the whole DataFrame as one single group and returns exactly one row
It raises an error, since agg() requires a groupBy() first
It returns one row per original row in the DataFrame
It automatically groups by every column in the DataFrame
questions.explain: This is the PySpark equivalent of a direct Pandas Series aggregate like df["fare_amount"].mean() from Lesson 23.

questions.q: What's the difference between count("*") and count("fare_amount")?
options: count("*") counts every row including nulls; count("fare_amount") counts only rows where fare_amount is not null
They always return exactly the same number
count("*") only works without groupBy(), while count("fare_amount") requires it
count("fare_amount") counts the number of unique values only
questions.explain: These can genuinely differ whenever Lesson 51's null handling left any gaps in fare_amount.

questions.q: Why does .alias() typically get used inside .agg() calls?
options: So the result has sensible, readable column names instead of Spark's default like sum(fare_amount)
alias() is required syntax and the call fails without it
It converts the aggregate result to a string type
It has no effect at all inside .agg() calls
questions.explain: Without it, the resulting column name is just the raw function call as text, which is much less readable.

questions.q: Where do sum(), avg(), max(), min(), and count() come from in PySpark?
options: pyspark.sql.functions — the same module as col() and when()
They are built directly into every DataFrame object with no import needed
Each one requires importing from a separate, uniquely-named module
They come from Python's built-in statistics module
questions.explain: This is the same single toolbox introduced across Lessons 44, 47, and 49 for building column expressions.
